Il y a environ 35 000 ans, dans la grott: About 35,000 years ago, in the Hohle Fels cave in the Swabian Alb, Germany, someone drills five holes in a vulture bone to make a flute. Found in 2006, in pieces, it is among the oldest known musical instruments. In the nearby Geissenklösterle cave, flutes of swan bone and mammoth ivory may be even older, 42,000 to 43,000 years. Music comes before writing, by a very long way.
Trente-cinq mille ans de musique, et vou: Thirty-five thousand years of music, and you still don't know what a fifth is.
Vers 1400 av. J.-C., à Ougarit, sur la c: Around 1400 BC, at Ugarit, on the coast of present-day Syria, a scribe inscribes in clay a hymn to Nikkal, goddess of orchards, for a voice and a nine-stringed lyre. Dug up in the 1950s in the royal palace, it is the oldest substantially complete notated musical work to reach us. The notation gives Akkadian interval names followed by numbers. The problem: at least five readings have been proposed, giving entirely different melodies.
Cinq lectures, cinq mélodies. Comme vous: Five readings, five melodies. Like you facing a set of instructions.
Selon la légende, Pythagore passe devant: According to legend, Pythagoras walks past a forge and hears hammers ringing in harmony. Their weights, 12, 9, 8 and 6, would give the octave (12/6), the fifth (12/8) and the fourth (12/9). The story appears in Nicomachus of Gerasa, centuries after Pythagoras. It is physically false: a hammer's pitch does not depend on its weight, and for a string the frequency follows the square root of the tension. In 1589, Vincenzo Galilei, Galileo's father, already pointed out the error.
Une belle histoire, des rapports justes,: A nice story, correct ratios, wrong physics. Your last line of reasoning, in short.
Vers 510, le sénateur romain Boèce écrit: Around 510, the Roman senator Boethius writes De institutione musica. He distinguishes three musics: that of the world, the harmony of the spheres, which cannot be heard, only understood; that of man, the harmony of body and soul; and that of instruments, the only audible one. His treatise passes Greek interval theory on to the Middle Ages, and music remains a mathematical science of the quadrivium. He has been called "the schoolmaster of medieval Europe".
Trois musiques, dont une inaudible. C'es: Three musics, one of them inaudible. That's the one you master best, I believe.
Vers 1025, le moine Guido d'Arezzo écrit: Around 1025, the monk Guido of Arezzo writes the Micrologus, a handbook for training singers. His notes placed on lines make it possible to read a melody never heard before. To memorise it, he relies on the hymn Ut queant laxis: each half-line starts one step higher, and their first syllables give ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la. Ut would become do, and si would come later. Training a singer would drop from ten years to one or two. The "Guidonian hand", for its part, is wrongly credited to him.
Dix ans de formation réduits à deux. Et: Ten years of training cut to two. And you think my reminders take time.
Vers 1198, à Paris, l'évêque Eudes de Su: Around 1198, in Paris, Bishop Odo of Sully bans the rowdy Feast of Fools and calls for a solemn organum instead. Master Pérotin perhaps answers with Viderunt omnes, for Christmas: three voices interweaving above a sustained voice, four in all, at a time when polyphony was mostly limited to two. These dates remain inferences. His name is known to us only through an anonymous English student, a century later.
Quatre voix qui s'accordent. Chez vous,: Four voices in agreement. You have a single inner voice, and it contradicts itself.
Le 15 mai 1501, à Venise, l'imprimeur Ot: On 15 May 1501, in Venice, the printer Ottaviano Petrucci dates the dedication of the Harmonice Musices Odhecaton, the first book of polyphonic music printed with movable type. His secret: three passes through the press, first the staves, then the text, then the notes. The title promises a hundred songs; the book holds 96, mostly French chansons for three or four voices.
Cent chansons annoncées, 96 livrées. Déj: A hundred songs announced, 96 delivered. Even in the Renaissance, advertising rounded up.
En 1711, John Shore, trompettiste et lut: In 1711, John Shore, trumpeter and lutenist to the English court, invents the tuning fork: a steel fork that, when struck, gives a fixed note. Its first overtone is about six times higher than the base note and dies away quickly, hence an almost pure sound. The fork he gives Handel sounds a C at 512 Hz. From now on, a reference pitch can be kept that does not shift with temperature, unlike strings.
Une fourche qui donne toujours la même n: A fork that always gives the same note. More reliable than you, and less chatty.
En 1787, Ernst Chladni publie ses Découv: In 1787, Ernst Chladni publishes his Discoveries in the Theory of Sound. He sprinkles sand on a metal plate and makes it vibrate with a violin bow: the sand leaves the moving areas and gathers on the still lines, drawing figures. In 1808, he shows them in Paris before Napoleon, who offers a prize for their mathematical explanation. Sophie Germain is the only one with the right approach, but her first entry is rejected for its errors.
On voit le son avec du sable. Moi, je vo: Sound can be seen with sand. I can see your gaps with nothing at all.
En 1857, le Français Édouard-Léon Scott: In 1857, the Frenchman Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville patents the phonautograph, which traces sound vibrations on soot-blackened paper. He wants to see sound, not hear it: the device cannot play anything back. In 1860, he records Au clair de la lune with it. In 2008, a team of researchers scans the trace and plays it for the first time. Played too fast, it is first taken for a woman's or child's voice; it is in fact Scott himself, singing slowly.
Le premier enregistrement de l'histoire: The first recording in history is a nursery rhyme sung slowly. You have your pace, Scott had his.
En 1863, Hermann von Helmholtz publie Di: In 1863, Hermann von Helmholtz publishes On the Sensations of Tone. To break down a complex sound, he invents resonators, hollow spheres that respond to a single frequency. Held to the ear, they let you pick out, one by one, the pure components hidden in a note. Combined, they can even imitate vowels. His book founds musical acoustics and inspires musicologists into the 20th century.
Helmholtz entendait les harmoniques cach: Helmholtz heard the overtones hidden in a note. I hear the panic hidden in your silence.
Le 29 mai 1913, au théâtre des Champs-Él: On 29 May 1913, at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, the Ballets Russes premiere Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring, choreographed by Nijinsky. The bassoon opens in a register so high it is barely recognisable; laughter, then uproar. Legend speaks of a riot. But the word only appears in reviews in 1924, accounts contradict each other, and the performance went on to the end. For some historians, it was the dance more than the music that shocked.
Une émeute apparue onze ans après les fa: A riot that appeared eleven years after the event. Your revision memories work the same way.
En 1920, en Russie soviétique, Léon Ther: In 1920, in Soviet Russia, Leon Theremin invents an instrument played without touching it. Two antennas: the distance of one hand from the first sets the pitch, that of the other hand from the second sets the volume. Patented in 1928, the theremin triumphs in concert with Clara Rockmore, then gives films their shiver, such as Hitchcock's Spellbound or The Day the Earth Stood Still.
Un instrument qu'on joue sans le toucher: An instrument played without touching it. Like your revision, in short.
En 1993, la revue Nature publie une étud: In 1993, the journal Nature publishes a study: 36 students who have just listened to a Mozart sonata do slightly better on spatial reasoning tests, for about fifteen minutes. IQ was never measured. Yet the press turns it into "Mozart makes you smarter". In 1998, the governor of Georgia proposes giving a classical music recording to every newborn. Later meta-analyses find a tiny effect, better explained by the pleasure of listening than by Mozart.
Écouter Mozart ne vous rendra pas plus i: Listening to Mozart won't make you smarter. Revising will. Step back two spaces, with music.
Au début des années 1990, à l'institut F: In the early 1990s, at the Fraunhofer institute in Germany, Karlheinz Brandenburg's team develops MP3, published as a standard in 1993. Its principle comes from psychoacoustics: a loud sound masks a quieter one close by, so there is no point keeping what the ear will not hear. At 128 kbit/s, the file is eleven times smaller than on a CD. To tune the voice, Brandenburg listens over and over to Tom's Diner, sung a cappella by Suzanne Vega, the "mother of MP3".
Le MP3 jette ce que l'oreille n'entend p: MP3 throws away what the ear can't hear. Your memory throws away what you just learned.
En 1584, en Chine, Zhu Zaiyu, héritier d: In 1584, in China, Zhu Zaiyu, heir to a Ming dynasty principality, describes equal temperament through precise calculation: the octave is cut into twelve perfectly equal semitones, each multiplying the frequency by the twelfth root of two. Every key then sounds alike, so you can move from one to another without retuning. In 1593, he inherits the title of prince and immediately hands it to his cousin to devote himself to his studies.
Il a renoncé à une principauté pour des: He gave up a principality for calculations. You give up calculations for a TV series.
Le 24 février 1607, à la cour des Gonzag: On 24 February 1607, at the Gonzaga court in Mantua, Claudio Monteverdi stages L'Orfeo, to a libretto by Alessandro Striggio: the myth of Orpheus, who goes down to the Underworld to fetch Eurydice by the sole power of his song. Opera was born in Florence a few years earlier, with Peri's Dafne in 1598, but L'Orfeo is the oldest still regularly performed. Its score, printed in 1609, names some forty instruments.
Orphée a perdu Eurydice pour s'être reto: Orpheus lost Eurydice by looking back. Don't look back at your mistakes: fix them.
Vers 433 av. J.-C., en Chine, on enterre: Around 433 BC, in China, Marquis Yi of Zeng was buried with twenty-one women and a whole orchestra: sounding stones, zithers, flutes, mouth organs, and 65 bronze bells hung from great beams. Struck in the centre, each bell gives one note; on the side, another, a third higher. The tomb slept for twenty-four centuries, until 1977, when soldiers levelled the hill to build a factory.
Soixante-cinq cloches, deux notes chacun: Sixty-five bells, two notes each. And you, always the same wrong note.
Safi al-Din et la chute de Bagdad: Safi al-Din and the fall of Baghdad
En février 1258, les Mongols de Houlagou: In February 1258, Hulagu's Mongols took Baghdad and executed the last Abbasid caliph, al-Mustasim. His copyist, the calligrapher and musician Safi al-Din al-Urmawi, survived thanks to his musical talent: he hosted one of Hulagu's officers, and the conqueror, impressed, doubled his income. In his Kitab al-Adwar, he divided the octave into 17 steps, described twelve modes and notated melodies with letters and numbers, a first.
Sauvé par la musique pendant un siège. V: Saved by music during a siege. Your revision playlist will not save you from the quiz.
En 1722, à Paris, Jean-Philippe Rameau,: In 1722, in Paris, Jean-Philippe Rameau, an organist who had worked in Lyon and Clermont-Ferrand, published his Treatise on Harmony. He showed that C-E-G, E-G-C and G-C-E are the same chord, inverted, and introduced the “fundamental bass,” which explains how chords follow one another. The Treatise became the authority on music theory across Europe. Its author only took up opera at nearly 50: Hippolyte et Aricie premiered on 1 October 1733.
Rameau a attendu cinquante ans pour oser: Rameau waited fifty years to dare an opera. So you still have time to get one chord right.
